newsitem.title: USA: Police need more tests on Red Wings limo driver.
newsitem.headline: Police need more tests on Red Wings limo driver.

text.p: Police said on Wednesday they had ordered more toxicology tests on the driver of a limousine that crashed, injuring members of the Detroit Red Wings hockey team -- meaning it will be early July before prosecutors decide whether to bring charges.

Red Wings defenceman Vladimir Konstantinov and team masseur Sergei Mnatsakanov suffered severe head injuries when the limo veered off a busy road and crashed into a tree on June 13 in a suburb of Detroit.

A third passenger, defenceman Slava Fetisov, was released from the hospital last week after sustaining chest contusions and a bruised lung. The crash came six days after the Red Wings won their first Stanley Cup championship in 42 years.

Based on witness reports and comments from limo driver Richard Gnida, police believe Gnida fell asleep. Hospital officials have said alcohol was not a factor. Police have also ruled out mechanical failure after accident investigators said the brakes met specifications.
"It appears to be purely a one-car-left-the-roadway accident with a driver who at this time appeared to doze off," said Birmingham Deputy Police Chief Richard Patterson.

At the time of the crash, Gnida was driving with a revoked license. He has a lengthy history of driving infractions. Patterson said Gnida had retained an attorney and had refused to talk to police since the accident.

Patterson declined on Wednesday to discuss initial blood test results on Gnida. Results from additional toxicology tests will take two weeks to complete. Police plan to present their investigation file to prosecutors on July 7.

Gnida will be charged with driving without a license, Patterson said. Additional charges could range from careless driving, which carries a small fine, to felonious driving, a two-year felony punishable by up to two years in jail and a fine of $1,000.

Officials at William Beaumont Hospital in Royal Oak, Michigan, said on Wednesday Konstantinov and Mnatsakanov were still in comas in critical condition. Doctors said earlier that both men continued to show small signs of improvement by displaying eye and hand movements in response to commands.
Doctors have started the process of taking Konstantinov off a ventilator and have removed an intercranial pressure monitor. Mnatsakanov's intercranial pressure continues to be monitored.
